reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
clinicalPearls: Fascioliasis is caused by the liver flukes Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica, primarily parasites of sheep and cattle that also infect humans worldwide, with high-burden foci in the Andes, Nile valley and parts of Asia
Humans are infected by eating aquatic plants such as watercress, or drinking water, contaminated with encysted metacercariae
The acute (hepatic/migratory) phase reflects larval migration through the liver parenchyma and causes fever, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly and marked eosinophilia
The chronic (biliary) phase occurs once adult flukes reside in the bile ducts, causing biliary colic, obstruction, cholangitis and sometimes obstructive jaundice
During the acute phase stool ova are absent because the flukes are not yet egg-laying, so serology is the diagnostic test of choice; eggs appear in stool or bile only in the chronic phase
Imaging in the acute phase may show hypodense migratory tracks or nodules in the liver, and eosinophilia is a key clue
Triclabendazole is the preferred agent for fascioliasis, and notably praziquantel is ineffective against Fasciola, unlike most other trematode infections
reference.pathophysiology: Ingested metacercariae excyst in the duodenum and the immature flukes penetrate the intestinal wall, cross the peritoneal cavity and burrow through the liver capsule and parenchyma over several weeks, producing necrotic migratory tracks and an intense eosinophilic inflammatory response that underlies the acute phase. The flukes then enter the bile ducts and mature into adults, where they cause chronic mechanical and inflammatory biliary injury, ductal hyperplasia, fibrosis and obstruction. Egg production begins only after maturation, explaining the diagnostic gap in the acute phase. Ectopic migration can rarely deposit flukes in other tissues.
additionalDifferentials: Other liver flukes (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis) in the chronic phase
Biliary stones and other causes of obstructive jaundice or cholangitis
Hypereosinophilic syndromes and other tissue-migrating helminths (e.g. toxocariasis)
additionalInvestigations: Serology (antibody detection) as the key test in the acute pre-patent phase
Stool microscopy for characteristic large operculated eggs in the chronic phase (with concentration)
Bile or duodenal aspirate examination for eggs when stool is negative
Liver function tests to assess cholestasis
Abdominal ultrasound, CT or MRI showing migratory tracks (acute) or biliary flukes and dilatation (chronic)
redFlags: Acute cholangitis with fever, jaundice and abdominal pain
Obstructive jaundice from adult flukes in the bile ducts
Severe acute-phase illness with high fever and marked systemic symptoms
Ectopic migration causing lesions outside the hepatobiliary system
Failure to respond, given regional triclabendazole resistance concerns
reference.prognosis: Most infections respond well to appropriate anthelmintic therapy with full recovery, but heavy or long-standing chronic infection can cause biliary fibrosis and recurrent cholangitis, and emerging triclabendazole resistance is a growing concern in some regions.
pitfalls: Relying on stool microscopy during the acute phase, when eggs are not yet produced, and missing the diagnosis
Using praziquantel, which is ineffective against Fasciola, instead of triclabendazole
Overlooking dietary exposure such as wild watercress ingestion
Mistaking acute-phase hepatic lesions for abscess or malignancy on imaging
Not considering treatment failure due to regional drug resistance
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
